finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id never awaits the authorization check, so any caller (including unauthenticated) can delete any report.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled req.params.id (server.js:19) and any request to DELETE /reports/:id, with or without a session.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; may be undefined for anonymous callers.
Handler loads report via attacker-chosen id.
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returned promise discarded.
authorize can only reject (403, or TypeError when req.user is undefined); rejection is not observed by the handler.
remove executes regardless of grant result.
Responds 204 Deleted.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() would throw 403 on missing grant but the throw never reaches the handler (missing await); no route-level auth middleware; no try/catch or error middleware in handler.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. authorize() (server.js:9-16) is async and throws a 403 on a missing grant, but the call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await, no .catch, and no try/catch in the handler (server.js:18-23). The rejection is unobserved, and the handler proceeds to db.reports.remove at server.js:21 regardless. No route-level auth middleware exists; the only middleware (server.js:4-7) just copies req.session.user.
verdict.reason: Every trace line checks out: authorize is async (server.js:9), its rejection is discarded because server.js:20 lacks await, and server.js:21 runs the delete unconditionally, so an anonymous or low-privilege caller can delete any report as long as the request reaches the route. Caveat: server.js:5 reads req.session.user with no session middleware in this file, so the route is only reachable if session middleware is supplied elsewhere; db is also undefined here, which suggests this is a fragment. The defect itself is real as written, and the candidate omits that unhandled rejection can crash the process on Node 15+.

finding.claim: The unawaited authorize() rejection is an unhandled promise rejection, which on Node >= 15 (default --unhandled-rejections=throw) terminates the process, giving an unauthenticated denial of service.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated or unauthorized DELETE /reports/:id request (req.user undefined or grant missing).
finding.sink: Process crash from unhandled rejection of authorize() at server.js:20.

trace.note: req.user undefined for anonymous request.
db.grants(user.id, ...) throws TypeError because user is undefined; or lines 11-14 throw 403.
Resulting rejected promise is neither awaited nor caught.
Node runtime terminates the server on unhandled rejection, taking down all routes.

finding.guards_checked: No process.on('unhandledRejection') handler in this file; Express version unknown (no package.json). Crash does not depend on Express because the promise is floating, not returned from the handler. Runtime version must be confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only candidate control is the authorize() check at server.js:20, but its result is never awaited or caught, so a rejection is never handled. No process.on('unhandledRejection') handler exists in server.js:1-33. No try/catch wraps the call.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 the un-awaited authorize() rejects for an anonymous request (req.user undefined at server.js:5, so user.id throws at server.js:10) or for a user lacking the grant (server.js:11-14 throw 403), and nothing handles that rejection, so on Node >= 15 with default unhandled-rejection mode the process exits. Caveats: the Node version is not confirmed by the code, and db is not defined in this file. Separately, and more serious than the candidate's claim: because line 20 is not awaited, line 21 (db.reports.remove) runs before the grant check resolves for any user with a defined but ungranted user object, so the DELETE is effectively unauthorized, not just a crash.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update, enabling mass assignment of protected fields (e.g. owner, id, permission fields) by any user holding the 'write' grant.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body req.body (server.js:3 express.json()), reachable by any user with 'write' on the report.
finding.sink: db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) (server.js:28), a persistent state change.

trace.note: express.json() parses body into req.body with no field allow-list.
Report loaded by attacker-chosen id.
await authorize(req.user, 'write', report) passes for a user with write grant.
Entire req.body written to the record.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() on 'write' is correctly awaited (line 27), so the access check works. No field whitelist or schema validation on req.body. Whether protected fields are immutable depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the directory.

verdict.guard_found: none. authorize() (server.js:9-16) throws on a missing grant, and line 27 awaits it, so the access check is correct but it is not a field filter. No allow-list or schema validation sits between req.body (server.js:3) and the write at server.js:28.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (server.js:3, 26, 27, 28), and no control blocks a user with a 'write' grant from sending arbitrary keys into db.reports.update at server.js:28. Whether owner or permission fields are actually writable, and so whether this is more than write-level access, depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the directory, and the field names in the claim are not in this code.

finding.claim: No authentication enforcement: req.user is copied from the session without checking it exists, so anonymous requests reach the handlers and fail with server errors rather than 401.
finding.sink: authorize(req.user, ...) at server.js:20 and :27, and db.grants(user.id, ...) at server.js:10.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user (undefined without a session).
user.id dereference throws TypeError.
PUT path: rejection is unhandled in Express 4 (crash on Node >= 15) or becomes a 500 in Express 5.

finding.guards_checked: No auth middleware on any route. No check that req.session exists; if no session middleware is mounted, line 5 throws on every request.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. There is no auth middleware, and the only check is authorize() at server.js:9-16, which throws on failure. On the DELETE route, that throw is never observed because server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the rejection is unhandled and server.js:21 runs db.reports.remove regardless.
verdict.reason: The candidate's claim that anonymous requests "fail with server errors rather than 401" is wrong for DELETE: server.js:20 omits await, so the TypeError from user.id (server.js:10) becomes an unhandled rejection and server.js:21-22 still delete the report and return 204, which is a real authorization bypass the candidate's trace does not describe (the PUT path at server.js:27 does fail with a 500 as claimed).

finding.claim: Missing-resource handling: for an unknown id, report is undefined and authorize()/report.id throws, returning a generic error instead of 404 and revealing that the id does not exist.
finding.sink: Error response or process behavior at server.js:10, :21, :28.

trace.note: db.reports.get returns undefined/null for unknown id.
authorize reads resource.id (or line 27 for PUT), throwing TypeError.
Response or crash depends on Express version (see F4).

finding.guards_checked: No null check on report after db.reports.get; no error-handling middleware.

verdict.guard_found: none. No try/catch or error-handling middleware in server.js, and no null check on report after db.reports.get (server.js:19, :26). The authorize() call at server.js:20 is not awaited, so its rejection is not caught there either.
verdict.reason: The trace is misdescribed: server.js:10 is db.grants(), not a response or crash point, and the TypeError from resource.id is raised inside async authorize() (server.js:10), not thrown at server.js:20, which is an unawaited call. The core defect is real: an unknown id leads to report being undefined at server.js:19 with no 404 path. Whether the result is a 500, a hung request, or a process crash depends on the Express version (F4), which this directory does not establish, so the existence-oracle impact cannot be settled from the code available.
